newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Bullish Swedish forecasts cheer markets.
newsitem.headline: Bullish Swedish forecasts cheer markets.

text.p: Two bullish reports on the Swedish economy were released by Wednesday, giving the markets an early dose of Christmas cheer, but analysts sounded a note of caution for the next two years.

A central bank commissioned survey of money market players and industry groups by researcher Prospera AB showed the business sector had lowered its inflationary expectations over the past three months.

This was followed by a report from Swedish government think-tank KI saying a dip in economic growth would be short and shallow. It saw Gross Domestic Product rising 2.7 percent in 1997 and 2.4 percent 1998 against 1.5 percent this year.

"A joyful message ahead of Christmas for the Riksbank," one analyst said. "But the risk is now above all that wage increases will not be in line with inflation if we get an economic upturn in 1997 and 1998."
Analysts said the bullish figures should allow the central bank, Riksbank, to continue lowering interest rates.

The market was widely expecting the Riksbank to lower its deposit and lending rates at a board meeting on Thursday and again trim its key interest and central rate, the repo, later this month for the 25th time this year.
"This bodes well for a new lowering in the repo rate on December 17 (when the Riksbank release its next inflation report)," said Swedbank analyst Knut Hallberg.
Prospera's survey, one of the Riksbank's key analytical tools, forecast annualised inflation at 1.4 percent in a year's time, 1.6 percent in two years and 2.0 percent in five years.
These figures were 20 basis points lower than the results of a similar survey carried out in September.

Wike Groenenberg, Salomon Bros economist, said she was not surprised by the softer inflation forecasts because of the inclusion of mortgage interest payments in the consumer price index which links interest rates falls into the measure.

"If the Riksbank cuts rates further and leaves rates low in 1997 - which is what I expect - this component will continue to depress consumer price inflation in 1997 and also producer prices," Groenenberg told Reuters.
"But I think the Swedish market, not just in 1998 but also in 1997, will be vulnerable to temporary set-backs."
Some analysts were sceptical about KI's growth forecast.
In its last forecast in August, KI forecast GDP rising 2.2 percent in 1997. It had not released forecasts for 1998 before.
Nordbanken economist Olle Djerf said KI painted too bright a picture about the Swedish domestic economy and a strong crown would continue to cap export growth.
"We don't think the private consumption is going to increase as KI says (at 2.5 percent in both 1997 and 1998)," Djerf told Reuters.
"We think there are bigger risks for turmoil in 1998 because we're approaching the moment of truth for EMU (Europe's economic and monetary union) as well as elections in France, Germany and Sweden.
"There are probably going to be some measures to cut unemployment (currently running at eight percent). That may worry the market."
